questions.stem: This action potential tracing lacks a stable resting membrane potential and shows a spontaneous, gradual phase 4 depolarization that drifts up to threshold. Which cardiac cell type does it represent?

explanation.summary: Only nodal (pacemaker) cells lack a true resting potential and undergo automatic phase 4 depolarization driven by the funny current (If) through HCN channels, followed by a calcium-dependent phase 0 (ICa) and potassium-dependent phase 3 (IK). Working myocytes and Purkinje fibers have a stable resting potential and a fast Na+-dependent upstroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only nodal (pacemaker) cells lack a true resting potential and undergo automatic phase 4 depolarization driven by the funny current (If) through HCN channels, followed by a calcium-dependent phase 0 (ICa) and potassium-dependent phase 3 (IK). Working myocytes and Purkinje fibers have a stable resting potential and a fast Na+-dependent upstroke.

questions.stem: In this pacemaker action potential the drug-modified (dark) curve shows a decreased slope of phase 4 depolarization and prolonged repolarization at the AV node compared with normal. Which drug mechanism produces this change?

explanation.summary: Class II antiarrhythmics (beta-blockers) inhibit sympathetic beta-1 stimulation of nodal cells, flattening the slope of phase 4 depolarization. This slows the firing rate of the SA node and conduction through the AV node, producing bradycardia and a prolonged PR interval.
explanation.whyCorrect: Class II antiarrhythmics (beta-blockers) inhibit sympathetic beta-1 stimulation of nodal cells, flattening the slope of phase 4 depolarization. This slows the firing rate of the SA node and conduction through the AV node, producing bradycardia and a prolonged PR interval.

questions.stem: The drug-modified (dark) curve overlaid on this nodal action potential shows a slowed rise of phase 0 and prolonged repolarization at the AV node. Blockade of which ionic current best explains the slowed upstroke?

explanation.summary: Nodal cells depend on L-type calcium influx for their phase 0 upstroke. Class IV agents (verapamil, diltiazem) block these L-type calcium channels, slowing depolarization and conduction through the AV node (negative dromotropy), which reduces heart rate and prolongs the PR interval.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nodal cells depend on L-type calcium influx for their phase 0 upstroke. Class IV agents (verapamil, diltiazem) block these L-type calcium channels, slowing depolarization and conduction through the AV node (negative dromotropy), which reduces heart rate and prolongs the PR interval.

questions.stem: In this posterior external view of the heart, the vessels highlighted in yellow entering the upper chamber are the single most common anatomical source of the ectopic electrical triggers that initiate a specific supraventricular arrhythmia. Which arrhythmia is that?

explanation.summary: The yellow-highlighted vessels are the pulmonary veins draining into the left atrium. Ectopic foci at the pulmonary vein ostia are the most common trigger for atrial fibrillation, which is why pulmonary vein isolation is the cornerstone of AF ablation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The yellow-highlighted vessels are the pulmonary veins draining into the left atrium. Ectopic foci at the pulmonary vein ostia are the most common trigger for atrial fibrillation, which is why pulmonary vein isolation is the cornerstone of AF ablation.

questions.stem: This tracing demonstrates a coarse fibrillatory baseline (best appreciated in lead V1) together with an irregularly irregular QRS response. What is the approximate atrial depolarization rate characteristic of this rhythm?

explanation.summary: In atrial fibrillation, multiple simultaneous reentrant wavelets produce a chaotic atrial rate exceeding 350 per minute. The AV node filters these impulses irregularly, producing the irregularly irregular ventricular response seen here.
explanation.whyCorrect: In atrial fibrillation, multiple simultaneous reentrant wavelets produce a chaotic atrial rate exceeding 350 per minute. The AV node filters these impulses irregularly, producing the irregularly irregular ventricular response seen here.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a beat whose P wave arrives early and has a different shape from the preceding sinus P waves, yet is followed by a normal narrow QRS. Which arrhythmia does this tracing best represent?

explanation.summary: An early, abnormally shaped (ectopic) P wave that is still conducted through the AV node to produce a normal narrow QRS is the hallmark of a premature atrial contraction. A PVC would show a wide QRS with no preceding P wave.
explanation.whyCorrect: An early, abnormally shaped (ectopic) P wave that is still conducted through the AV node to produce a normal narrow QRS is the hallmark of a premature atrial contraction. A PVC would show a wide QRS with no preceding P wave.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows organized sawtooth atrial waves at a constant rate, but the spacing between QRS complexes varies from beat to beat. What accounts for the irregular ventricular response seen here?

explanation.summary: In atrial flutter the atrial (flutter) rate is fixed; when the AV node conducts at changing ratios (e.g. alternating 2:1 and 4:1) the ventricular rhythm becomes irregular even though the atrial rate is constant.
explanation.whyCorrect: In atrial flutter the atrial (flutter) rate is fixed; when the AV node conducts at changing ratios (e.g. alternating 2:1 and 4:1) the ventricular rhythm becomes irregular even though the atrial rate is constant.

questions.stem: This ECG from a patient with chronic lung disease shows an irregular tachycardia in which the P waves (arrows) have at least three distinct shapes. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Three or more distinct P-wave morphologies with an irregular rate over 100/min define multifocal atrial tachycardia, seen most often with pulmonary disease. Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves.
explanation.whyCorrect: Three or more distinct P-wave morphologies with an irregular rate over 100/min define multifocal atrial tachycardia, seen most often with pulmonary disease. Atrial fibrillation lacks discrete organized P waves.

questions.stem: This ECG shows an abrupt regular narrow-complex tachycardia in which a retrograde P wave is buried just after each QRS. In young, otherwise healthy patients this rhythm is most commonly caused by which mechanism?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reentry through dual AV nodal pathways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reentry over an accessory bypass tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhanced automaticity of an atrial focus

explanation.summary: AVNRT is a micro-reentrant circuit using fast and slow pathways within the AV node, producing a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave close to the QRS. It is the most common SVT in young people.
explanation.whyCorrect: AVNRT is a micro-reentrant circuit using fast and slow pathways within the AV node, producing a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with a retrograde P wave close to the QRS. It is the most common SVT in young people.

questions.stem: This schematic contrasts a normal QRS with one that has a slurred upstroke at its onset and a shortened PR interval. What underlying electrophysiologic event produces this waveform change?

explanation.summary: The slurred initial upstroke (delta wave) with a short PR interval reflects early ventricular depolarization arriving through an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node, i.e. pre-excitation as in WPW.
explanation.whyCorrect: The slurred initial upstroke (delta wave) with a short PR interval reflects early ventricular depolarization arriving through an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node, i.e. pre-excitation as in WPW.

questions.stem: This baseline (sinus rhythm) 12-lead ECG shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS complexes (arrows). What does this finding indicate?

explanation.summary: The short PR interval plus delta waves during sinus rhythm signify ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory (Kent) bundle, the defining ECG signature of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The short PR interval plus delta waves during sinus rhythm signify ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory (Kent) bundle, the defining ECG signature of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
